items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: Like Elvin Jones used to tell me, he says, “McBee, if you don’t hear anything... play that.”

ctx.x: It reminds me, I recently was talking to a younger bass player and we were talking about bass solos and he expressed that he would get quite aggravated when it was time for the bass solo and everybody else just stopped. You know like okay, a cappella, it’s all on you and there’s no accompaniment and no support. And I wonder when you have your choice what do you like to have happen behind your bass solo?

Behind my bass solo — well first of all, if in tempo, the piano must sustain chords to support me. Don’t rhythmatize anything. Don’t play rhythmically you know. Just sustain, so I can have a carpet, I can hear where the changes are going. But other than that, it’s important to be able to express regardless of the situation. Like Elvin Jones used to tell me, he says, “McBee, if you don’t hear anything, if you don’t have anything to play, if you don’t feel nothing,” he says, “play that.”

items.title: Mcbee interviewed by Monk Rowe, 2020
items.q: I would become friends with Yusef Lateef, with Elvin Jones, with Paul Chambers, people like that that would be there occasionally.

ctx.x: Yeah. Can you describe for us what that was like? What would the tunes be? And was the function of it partly to meet people, to maybe find gigs and just improve yourself?

No. The function of it, mind you I’m the young guy. I’m just there you know. I’m out of the exterior if you will. The function of it was to touch base. The musicians that would gather there each and every Sunday that might be in town or might be at home, but just meet and have a good time playing music. So what? It wasn’t about having a gig or anything like that. Because as I mentioned before on the way to New York, now that I’m out of the Army where I practiced my bass every night until three or four in the…
Did you join the military or were you drafted?
